extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of federal education funding (postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, institutional legal counsel, and higher-education administrators
extracted.subtask_short: Title IX jurisdiction and response standards
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance on (1) the scope/jurisdictional limits of 'education program or activity' under Title IX (including geographic/extraterritorial limits) and (2) the required recipient response standard (deliberate indifference), supportive measures, and related procedural obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'education program or activity' (scope/jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of §§ 106.30, 106.44, and 106.45, 'education program or activity' includes locations, events, or circumstances over which the respondent had substantial control over both the respondent and the context in which the sexual harassment occurred, and also includes buildings owned or controlled by student organizations that are officially recognized by a postsecondary institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a jurisdictional limitation (not a geographic test). Whether conduct occurred 'in' an education program or activity is a fact-specific inquiry focused on whether the recipient exercised substantial control over the respondent and the context. The rule clarifies that recognized student-organization-owned/controlled buildings can be covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: No bright-line geographic test; off-campus/online conduct not categorically excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'education program or activity' limitation does not create or apply a geographic test and does not draw a line between 'off campus' and 'on campus,' nor between in-person and online harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Off-campus sexual misconduct can be covered if the recipient had substantial control over the respondent and the context. The inquiry is fact-specific; recipients should not assume off-campus or online incidents are automatically outside Title IX. Training is required to help staff understand scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Against a person in the United States' (extraterritoriality) limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.44(a) applies only where alleged sexual harassment occurred 'against a person in the United States.' Title IX, by its plain text, does not have extraterritorial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This jurisdictional limitation means alleged misconduct occurring when the complainant was located outside the U.S. is outside Title IX enforcement scope. However, recipients remain free (and are encouraged) to address such misconduct through their own codes of conduct and to offer supportive measures; dismissal under Title IX for extraterritorial conduct is 'only for purposes of Title IX.' Practical investigatory difficulties abroad (witnesses, evidence) inform this limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to investigate formal complaints within jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must investigate a formal complaint where the alleged sexual harassment (meeting the definition in § 106.30) occurred in the recipient's education program or activity, against a person in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients' decisions to investigate cannot be arbitrary. If the facts indicate the incident falls within the recipient's education program or activity and the complainant was in the United States, the recipient has a duty to investigate under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate indifference response standard (maintained, with specified actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will maintain the 'deliberate indifference' standard in the final regulations but has revised § 106.44(a) to specify certain actions a recipient must take in order to not be deliberately indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid being deliberately indifferent, a recipient's response must treat complainants and respondents equitably by offering supportive measures to complainants and by following a grievance process that complies with § 106.45 before imposing disciplinary sanctions or other actions that are not supportive measures against a respondent. The standard affords discretion but requires specific baseline actions; it is not a carte blanche to ignore complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures: offer and interactive process
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must offer supportive measures (as defined in § 106.30) to a complainant, and the Title IX Coordinator must promptly contact the complainant to discuss availability, consider the complainant's wishes, inform of availability with or without filing a formal complaint, and explain the process for filing a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should engage in a meaningful dialogue (interactive process) to determine which supportive measures may restore or preserve equal access without unreasonably burdening the other party. A recipient must offer supportive measures to each complainant; the obligation is sufficiently fulfilled so long as the offer is not 'clearly unreasonable' in light of the known circumstances. There may be practical limits (e.g., anonymous reports where the complainant cannot be contacted). Supportive measures may be provided with or without a formal complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural protection before disciplinary sanctions (grievance process compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must follow a grievance process that complies with § 106.45 before imposing any disciplinary sanctions or other non-supportive measures against a respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves fairness and notice for respondents (and complainants) — respondents should not be punished until after completion of a § 106.45-compliant grievance process. The requirement is part of what constitutes a non-deliberately indifferent response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirement on scope of education program or activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised § 106.45(b)(1)(iii) requires training for Title IX Coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, and persons who facilitate informal resolution processes on 'the scope of the recipient's education program or activity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must ensure relevant personnel understand how to apply the substantial-control / program-or-activity analysis, including how off-campus and online incidents may fall within Title IX. Training is a required element to ensure consistent application of jurisdictional rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent terminology: use 'in' (interchangeable with 'under')
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations replace 'within' with 'in' throughout, and the Department treats 'in' as interchangeable with the Title IX statute's use of 'under.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This drafting consistency clarifies that 'in' and 'under' are intended to have the same meaning for jurisdictional coverage; recipients should apply the same interpretive standard regardless of prior usage of 'within/under/in' terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient discretion to address conduct outside Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations prohibits recipients from using their own disciplinary processes to address misconduct occurring outside the recipient's education program or activity; recipients may also offer supportive measures for such misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where Title IX does not apply (e.g., extraterritorial incidents or incidents outside the recipient's program/activity), institutions retain authority to investigate, discipline, and provide supports under their own conduct codes. Dismissal under Title IX as outside scope does not prevent institutional action.
